afraid, quite sure of ourselves and of our life. This does not
mean of course to be simply freed from pain and anxiety,
nor even to be no longer pressed by questions and problems,
as they constantly confront us in the duties of our life and in
our fate. But it does mean that in our inner being we cease
to be ambiguous, with the result that all anxiety and pain,
all questions and problems have lost their sting for us; that
they no longer have any power to assail us; that in calm
and cheerful self-certitude we rise above their buffeting.
II
This "light of life" Jesus promises to them who follow
Him. The price to be paid for the gift is that of discipleship.
What does this mean? At bottom it means nothing other
than truly to desire what is promised. The peculiar feature
here is that the word of promise is the word of judgment
also: "For judgment I came into this world, that those who
do not see may see and that those who see may become
blind." It is the very word of promise which is at the same
time a word declaratory of judgment; the gift itself, the
"light of life" effects judgment. For it effects a discrimination
between those who accept the gift and those who close their
hearts against it. The judgment that is here in question is not
a special arrangement for the end of time, but a process
consummated in the hearing of the gospel proclamation
itself. Elsewhere we read, "And this is the judgment, that
the light has come into the world and men loved darkness
rather than light" (John 3: 19).
This is very strange! Do we not all love light? Do we not
all long for the light of life, for that luminosity of existence
which enables us to be victorious over the world? No doubt
we all have a dim surmise and a passionate longing-how-
ever misunderstood-that we must somehow be delivered
from this world, from what is merely given and actual; a
feeling that the world can never give us an inexhaustible
